title: North Korea Banned This Korean Snack — The Wild Story of Choco Pie
description:
In 2014, North Korea reportedly banned a snack. Not a weapon, not a phone. A small round chocolate cake from South Korea. This is the wild life story of Choco Pie: born from a trip to Georgia, USA, turned into a soldier's currency in Korea's army, a tea-time hero in Russia, an offering on Vietnamese family altars, and a black-market treasure north of the border.

Chapters

Where did you eat your first Choco Pie? Tell us in the comments.

#ChocoPie #NorthKorea #WhatKoreaSays
sources: The Great Choco Pie War of 2014-2015 — Now I Know: https://nowiknow.com/?p=7814
Choco Pies in North Korea — NK Econ Watch: https://www.nkeconwatch.com/2015/07/14/south-koreas-subversive-chocko-pies/
Orion 2024 Choco Pie sales (overseas share ~86%) — Digital Daily / Hankyung, 2025-02-27
Orion Russia capacity and new Tver plant — Money Today, 2026-04-22

say: In 2014, North Korea reportedly banned something coming in from the South.
Not a weapon. Not a phone. Not a K-drama on a USB stick.
A snack. A small, round, chocolate-covered snack.
It's called Choco Pie. Two soft cakes, marshmallow in the middle, wrapped in chocolate.
In South Korea, it costs less than a cup of coffee. Every convenience store has it.
So how does a snack this ordinary end up worrying a government?
This little cake has lived a stranger life than most people.
It was invented after a trip to America. It became a kind of currency for Korean soldiers. It conquered Russia, ended up on family altars in Vietnam,
and at the end, it crossed into North Korea, where things got really strange.
Stay to the end, because the last part involves balloons. Ten thousand Choco Pies, floating over the most guarded border on earth.

scenes.title: A Korean snack born in Georgia
say: Let's start at the beginning. And the beginning is not in Korea.
In 1973, a researcher from a Korean confectionery company was traveling in the American South.
At a hotel in Georgia, he was served a chocolate-coated sweet with his coffee.
One bite, and he had an idea. What if Korea had a snack like this, cheap enough for anyone?
He brought the idea home, and the team started experimenting.
The next year, in 1974, Choco Pie hit Korean shelves.
Korea was still a poor country back then. A chocolate snack felt like a small luxury, something you'd save, or give to someone you cared about.
And that's where Choco Pie found its secret weapon. One Korean word: jeong.
Jeong is hard to translate. It's the warm, sticky feeling between people who've been through things together. Your grandma pushing food on you. A friend who shows up without being asked.
Orion printed that word right on the box. Choco Pie wasn't just a snack anymore. It was how you said, I care about you, without saying it.

scenes.title: Currency in the barracks
say: Which brings us to the most unlikely fan base of all. Korean soldiers.
In South Korea, almost every young man serves in the military for around a year and a half.
Life on base is strict, food is plain, and sweets are rare.
So a box of Choco Pies becomes something like money. You trade them. You share them. You owe someone a Choco Pie.

scenes.en: Soldiers go to Sunday religious services... for the free Choco Pies.
say: There's a famous joke that every Korean man knows.
Why do so many soldiers suddenly become religious on Sunday? Because the services hand out free Choco Pies.
Ask any Korean guy who served. Most of them will laugh, and then admit it's at least a little bit true.

scenes.title: Russia falls in love
say: Now, a snack that powerful was never going to stay inside Korea.
In the early nineteen-nineties, the Soviet Union had just collapsed. Shelves in Russia's far east were empty.
Russian traders started sailing to Korean ports like Busan, filling huge bags with anything they could resell back home.
And one of the things they kept buying, by the boxful, was Choco Pie.
It turned out to be a perfect match for Russia.
It doesn't need a fridge. It survives long train rides across Siberia. And it goes beautifully with a glass of hot tea, which is how many Russians end the day.
By twenty sixteen, Russians were buying around six hundred million packs a year.
Today Orion makes Choco Pies inside Russia, and the factories still can't keep up.
The lines have been running above their normal capacity, so the company is building a whole new factory building in the Tver region, northwest of Moscow, aiming to roughly double production.
Think about that. A Korean snack is so popular in Russia that they're running out of room to make it.

scenes.title: On the family altar in Vietnam
say: Next stop, Vietnam. And this is where Choco Pie got a promotion.
In Vietnam, families honor their ancestors during the Lunar New Year with an altar full of offerings.
Fruit, flowers, cakes. And in a lot of homes, a box of Choco Pie.
Orion translated jeong into a Vietnamese word, tình, meaning affection, and sold it as a gift that carries your feelings.
So in Korea, Choco Pie comforts homesick soldiers. In Vietnam, it's offered to great-grandparents. Not a bad career path for a cookie.
In China, the company did something even smarter.
Orion's Chinese name means good friend. And for Choco Pie, it swapped jeong for a different character, ren, a Confucian word for kindness and humanity.
Same snack. Three countries. Three different words for love. And today, China is actually Orion's biggest market, bigger than Korea itself.

scenes.title: The black market up north
say: Now we come to the strangest chapter. The one that got it banned.
Just north of the border, there used to be a place called the Kaesong Industrial Complex.
South Korean companies ran factories there, and North Korean workers worked in them. It was one of the only places where the two Koreas met every single day.
The companies weren't allowed to hand out extra cash. So as a bonus, they gave workers snacks. And the snack everyone wanted was Choco Pie.

scenes.label: reported black-market price of a single Choco Pie in North Korea (Chosun Ilbo, 2010)
say: Many workers didn't eat them. They took them home and sold them.
In twenty ten, a South Korean newspaper reported that a single Choco Pie could fetch as much as nine dollars and fifty cents on the North Korean black market.
For a snack that costs a few cents in Seoul.
For a regime that controls almost everything people see and hear, that was a problem.
Here was a sweet, cheap, delicious taste of the South, passed hand to hand across the country.
Some called it a taste of capitalism in a plastic wrapper.
So, according to reports in twenty fourteen, the factories were told to stop handing out Choco Pies, and give out things like sausages, instant noodles and coffee instead.
And remember the balloons I promised you?
That same year, South Korean activists tied ten thousand Choco Pies to giant helium balloons, and released them toward the North.
A snack, floating over the most heavily guarded border in the world. You honestly can't make this up.

items: Inspired by a hotel snack in Georgia, USA
Jeong: love you don't say out loud
say: So let's add it up.
A hotel snack in Georgia inspired it. A Korean word for love sold it. Soldiers traded it, Russians fell for it, Vietnamese families offered it to their ancestors,
and North Korea decided it was too dangerous to hand out.

scenes.label: of Choco Pie sales now come from outside Korea (Orion, 2024)
say: And here's the final twist.
Today, about eighty-six percent of Choco Pie's sales come from outside Korea.
The snack Koreans think of as theirs has quietly become one of the most well-traveled cakes on the planet.
So, where did you eat your first Choco Pie? Tell us in the comments. We're curious which country wins.
If you like strange true stories about Korea, subscribe. There are a lot more where this came from.
